item.title: Gross rental income rises to £90,000 for average landlord
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across the UK have seen their gross rental incomes rise substantially, with recent data suggesting the average property investor now earns approximately £90,000 annually from lettings. Whilst this marks a significant increase in revenue streams, industry analysts note that operating costs and mortgage expenses have also climbed, potentially affecting net profitability.

Rental market shows resilience despite economic pressures

The private rental sector continues to demonstrate strength, with gross yields growing as demand outstrips supply in many regions. Several factors contribute to this trend, including population growth, delayed first-time buyer purchases, and limited new housing stock. Landlords with multiple properties may find their combined rental income reaching the £90,000 average as market conditions favour established investors.

However, property owners should be aware that gross income figures don't reflect the full financial picture. Rising interest rates have increased mortgage repayments for those with variable or tracker deals, whilst maintenance costs and regulatory compliance expenses have similarly grown. Some buy-to-let investors might need to reassess their portfolios to maintain healthy profit margins.

Important considerations for landlords

For those evaluating their property investments, several key aspects warrant attention:

  • Tax implications: Higher rental income may push some landlords into different tax brackets, affecting overall profitability
  • Mortgage options: Remortgaging could help secure better rates amidst changing market conditions
  • Energy efficiency requirements: Upcoming EPC regulations may necessitate property upgrades
  • Insurance costs: Comprehensive landlord cover remains essential as premiums adjust to inflation

Professional property management services might appeal to investors seeking to streamline operations, though this comes at an additional cost that affects net returns. Portfolio landlords with multiple properties might consider diversifying their holdings across different regions to mitigate local market risks.

Whilst rising gross incomes present opportunities, prudent landlords will balance these against increasing outgoings to maintain sustainable rental businesses. Financial advice tailored to individual circumstances could prove valuable in navigating this complex landscape.

item.title: Fall in mortgage approvals reflects July price volatility
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Mortgage approvals experienced a noticeable dip in July, as fluctuating interest rates and economic uncertainty impacted buyer confidence and affordability. This downturn reflects the broader volatility in the property market, with potential homeowners and investors adopting a more cautious approach amidst the unpredictable financial landscape.

Impact of Rate Uncertainty on Mortgage Activity

The decline in mortgage approvals can be largely attributed to the ongoing uncertainty surrounding interest rates. With the Bank of England's base rate adjustments and lenders frequently revising their mortgage products, many borrowers may have paused their plans to secure a home loan. This hesitation is understandable, as rate changes can significantly affect monthly repayments and overall affordability.

First-time buyers and those looking to remortgage may have found themselves particularly vulnerable to these shifts. The fluctuating rates could have made it challenging to lock in a favourable deal, prompting some to delay their decisions until the market stabilises.

Affordability Concerns and Buyer Confidence

Affordability remains a key concern for many prospective homeowners, especially in light of rising living costs and inflation. The combination of higher mortgage rates and increased household expenses has placed additional financial pressure on buyers, leading to a more cautious approach to property purchases.

For those considering stepping onto the property ladder, the current climate may feel particularly daunting. The uncertainty surrounding future rate changes and the potential for further economic instability could be discouraging some from taking the plunge. Similarly, homeowners looking to remortgage might be weighing their options carefully, seeking to balance affordability with long-term financial security.

Looking Ahead: What Borrowers Might Consider

Whilst the current market presents challenges, there are steps borrowers might consider to navigate the volatility. Seeking advice from a mortgage broker could help identify the most suitable options based on individual circumstances. Additionally, keeping a close eye on rate trends and lender offers may enable borrowers to secure a competitive deal when the time is right.

For those able to proceed, fixed-rate mortgages could offer a sense of stability amidst the uncertainty. Locking in a rate for a set period might provide peace of mind, shielding borrowers from potential rate hikes in the near future.

As the property market continues to evolve, staying informed and seeking professional guidance could prove invaluable for those looking to make confident, well-informed decisions.

item.title: House prices down second month in a row
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

UK house prices have fallen for two consecutive months according to latest industry data, as affordability constraints and higher mortgage costs continue to impact buyer demand. The figures from Lloyds Banking Group suggest a cautious market sentiment amongst prospective purchasers facing ongoing financial pressures.

What the latest house price data shows

The recent dip marks the first back-to-back monthly decline in property values since early 2023, with analysts noting particular softening in regional markets outside London. Whilst annual growth remains positive across most areas, the monthly contraction indicates cooling demand as borrowers grapple with elevated interest rates and living costs.

Market observers highlight several factors influencing current conditions:

  • Mortgage rates remaining above 2021/2022 levels despite recent stabilisation
  • Ongoing affordability challenges for first-time buyers
  • Reduced buying power due to the cumulative effect of rising rates
  • Some homeowners choosing to delay moving plans

How this affects different market segments

The current conditions create varied impacts across different buyer groups. Existing homeowners with substantial equity may find they retain significant bargaining power, whilst first-time buyers continue facing deposit hurdles. Buy-to-let investors are reassessing yields as rental growth shows signs of slowing in some areas.

For those considering their next move, several approaches might be worth considering:

  • Monitoring local market trends rather than national averages
  • Seeking independent mortgage advice to understand borrowing capacity
  • Exploring different mortgage products that could suit changing circumstances
  • Being prepared for potentially longer sales completion timelines

As always in fluctuating markets, taking a measured approach and seeking professional financial guidance can help individuals make informed property decisions tailored to their personal circumstances.

item.title: Atom Bank launches funding for BNG habitat banks
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Atom Bank has introduced a new lending initiative aimed at supporting habitat creation projects, which could assist property developers in meeting Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) requirements. This move highlights the growing importance of sustainability and environmental considerations in the UK property and mortgage sectors.

What is Biodiversity Net Gain?

Biodiversity Net Gain is a policy introduced in England to ensure that development projects leave natural habitats in a better state than before. Under these regulations, developers are required to demonstrate a measurable increase in biodiversity, often achieved through habitat creation or enhancement. This approach aims to balance urban growth with environmental conservation, ensuring that wildlife and ecosystems are protected.

How Atom Bank’s Lending Initiative Works

Atom Bank’s new funding scheme focuses on providing financial support for habitat banks, which are areas designated for biodiversity enhancement. These habitat banks can help developers meet their BNG obligations by offsetting any ecological impact caused by their projects. By offering tailored financing solutions, Atom Bank aims to make it easier for developers to comply with environmental regulations whilst fostering sustainable development.

This initiative not only supports developers but also contributes to broader environmental goals. Habitat banks can play a crucial role in restoring natural landscapes, improving biodiversity, and mitigating the effects of climate change. For developers, access to such funding could streamline the planning process and reduce the complexity of meeting BNG requirements.

Why This Matters for the Property Sector

The introduction of this lending initiative reflects a broader trend in the property sector towards integrating environmental considerations into development projects. As sustainability becomes a key focus, developers and lenders alike are exploring innovative ways to align their activities with environmental goals. Atom Bank’s funding for habitat banks is an example of how financial institutions can play a role in promoting greener development practices.

For homeowners and property investors, this shift towards sustainable development could also have long-term benefits. Properties built with biodiversity in mind may appeal to environmentally conscious buyers and could potentially see increased demand in the future.

Atom Bank’s new lending initiative underscores the growing intersection of finance, property, and environmental sustainability. By supporting habitat creation and helping developers meet BNG requirements, this scheme highlights the importance of balancing economic growth with ecological preservation. Borrowers and developers alike might find value in exploring how such initiatives can support their goals whilst contributing to a greener future.

item.title: The growth of sustainable living and why successful investment starts with delivery
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The rise of sustainable living has become a significant trend in the UK property market, with homeowners increasingly prioritising eco-friendly features and energy-efficient homes. This shift reflects growing environmental awareness and the desire to reduce long-term living costs. However, for investors and developers, delivering sustainable properties that meet genuine demand requires careful planning, robust assets, and a commitment to long-term execution.

The appeal of sustainable living

Sustainable living is no longer a niche concept but a mainstream priority for many buyers and renters. Features such as solar panels, heat pumps, and improved insulation are becoming key selling points. Homeowners may find that investing in such properties not only aligns with their environmental values but also offers potential savings on utility bills. Additionally, government incentives and stricter energy efficiency regulations are further driving interest in eco-friendly homes.

Key factors for successful investment

For those considering investing in sustainable property, several factors could influence success. Firstly, understanding genuine market demand is crucial. Properties with sustainable features must cater to the needs and preferences of the target audience. Secondly, the quality of assets plays a vital role. High-performance materials and reliable eco-technologies can enhance a property’s appeal and longevity. Finally, effective delivery is essential. Projects must be completed on time and to a high standard to build trust and maximise returns.

The importance of long-term planning

Sustainable property investment often requires a forward-thinking approach. Developers and investors might consider the lifecycle of eco-friendly technologies and how they will perform over time. Regular maintenance and updates could be necessary to ensure properties remain efficient and attractive to future buyers or tenants. Long-term planning also involves staying informed about evolving regulations and technological advancements in the sustainable living sector.

As the demand for eco-friendly homes continues to grow, sustainable living presents both opportunities and challenges for the property market. By focusing on genuine demand, strong assets, and effective delivery, investors and homeowners alike could benefit from this burgeoning trend.

item.title: Letting agents in London face five-year high in tenant competition
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

London’s rental market has seen heightened competition among tenants this summer, reaching levels not witnessed in five years. A combination of dwindling supply and sustained demand has created a challenging environment for renters, particularly in prime outer London (POL). According to recent data from Rightmove and Knight Frank, the number of new rental listings across prime central London (PCL) and POL was 10% below the five-year average between June and August. This scarcity has been attributed to a series of tax and regulatory changes affecting landlords, including the Renters’ Rights Act introduced in May.

Declining Supply and Rising Demand

The shortage of rental properties has been a persistent issue since April 2021, with new listings consistently failing to exceed the five-year average. This decline in supply has been accompanied by an 8% drop in completed lettings across London compared to the same period last year. However, the market has shown contrasting trends at different price points. Properties priced above £1,000 per week saw a 13% increase in new listings compared to the five-year average, as discretionary owners opted to rent rather than sell in a weaker sales market.

Tenant competition has been particularly intense in POL, where there were 8.7 prospective renters for every new listing in August—the highest figure in five years. In contrast, PCL recorded 5.2 prospective tenants per listing, indicating a slightly less competitive environment. Rental growth also varied significantly by location, with POL experiencing a 3% increase in average rents over the year to August, compared to a modest 1.2% rise in PCL.

Super-Prime Market Remains Robust

At the higher end of the market, activity has remained strong. The number of super-prime tenancies—those priced above £5,000 per week—was 13% above the five-year average in the three months to August. Knight Frank noted that weakness in the high-value sales market has driven demand, with some prospective buyers choosing to rent instead of purchasing property. Tom Smith, head of super-prime lettings at Knight Frank, highlighted that many potential buyers are deferring purchasing decisions and opting to rent for an additional 12 to 24 months. Concerns around non-dom reforms and broader tax policies have also contributed to this cautious approach.

For tenants navigating this competitive landscape, understanding market dynamics could be crucial. With rental supply constrained and demand remaining high, renters might consider exploring a range of properties or seeking professional advice to secure suitable accommodation. Meanwhile, landlords may find opportunities in the upper end of the market, where flexibility and demand remain strong.

item.title: Why links and late documents will not help you at a rent tribunal
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiyawan

Recent changes to assured tenancy rules have introduced stricter requirements for landlords proposing rent increases. Since May 2026, rent adjustments must follow the statutory procedure using Form 4A, with tenants having the right to challenge increases through tribunal applications. A recent First Tier Tribunal case highlights the importance of adhering to these new regulations and proper tribunal procedures.

Understanding the rent tribunal process

Under the updated rules, tenants may request an open market rent determination if they believe a proposed increase is unreasonable. Applications must be made before the new rent takes effect, with new tenants having a six-month window to challenge initial rent levels. Landlords must now be prepared to justify their proposed rents with credible evidence, typically through comparable property data.

The case of 8 Pierhead Lock demonstrates how procedural missteps can significantly impact outcomes. When the landlord proposed increasing the rent from £2,700 to £3,100 monthly, the tenants successfully challenged this at tribunal, maintaining the original rate. The landlord's failure to submit the required Form MR2 and reliance on document links rather than complete evidence contributed to this decision.

Key lessons for landlords

This ruling offers several important reminders for landlords navigating the new rent determination process:

  • Submit all required documentation promptly: The tribunal dismissed the landlord's case partly due to the missing Form MR2, which serves as the formal response to tenant challenges. Landlords must ensure all paperwork is completed and submitted within the specified timelines.
  • Provide complete evidence, not just links: The tribunal explicitly stated it does not follow external links. Comparable property details and supporting documentation must be included within the formal submission rather than referenced indirectly.
  • Adhere to submission deadlines: Additional evidence submitted on the hearing day was disregarded due to lateness. Landlords should prepare their full case well in advance of tribunal dates.

While the focus of rent tribunals remains assessing fair market value, procedural compliance has become equally crucial under the new regulations. Landlords seeking rent increases may wish to familiarise themselves with the updated requirements and ensure they have robust supporting evidence prepared well before any potential tribunal dates. The Pierhead Lock case demonstrates how technical oversights, rather than the rent assessment itself, can determine outcomes in these proceedings.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The mortgage and property sectors continue to see notable movements as professionals shift roles and bring their expertise to new platforms. Two recent appointments highlight this trend, with experienced figures joining Moveli and Hampshire Trust Bank (HTB) in key positions.

George Henty-Dodd Joins Moveli

George Henty-Dodd, previously head of sales at John D Wood & Co in Parsons Green, has joined Moveli as a broker covering Fulham and surrounding areas. With nearly a decade of experience in London’s residential sales and lettings market, Henty-Dodd brings deep local knowledge to his new role. His career includes stints at Foxtons and Chestertons, where he honed his expertise in the SW6 property market.

At Moveli, Henty-Dodd will operate under the self-employed agent model, leveraging the company’s technology, marketing, and support services whilst maintaining his own brand. Moveli, which eschews traditional branch networks in favour of a broker-led approach, now boasts over 100 agents across London and other parts of the UK. Ben Littlewood, co-founder of Moveli, praised Henty-Dodd’s appointment, stating that his extensive experience and familiarity with Fulham make him an ideal addition to the growing network.

Dan Fyffe Appointed at Hampshire Trust Bank

In another significant move, Dan Fyffe has been appointed as lending director within HTB’s development finance team, focusing on the South. Fyffe brings over 20 years of banking experience, including 17 years in property and development finance. His career includes roles at Mizrahi Tefahot Bank, where he managed a portfolio of property clients, and Shawbrook Bank, where he played a pivotal role in establishing its development finance operation.

At HTB, Fyffe will work closely with brokers and SME property developers, drawing on his experience in structuring deals ranging from £1 million to £35 million. He highlighted HTB’s flexible and practical approach to development finance as a key factor in his decision to join the bank. Fyffe emphasised the importance of understanding the evolving needs of brokers and developers in a constantly changing market.

These appointments reflect broader trends in the industry, with professionals increasingly gravitating towards flexible, technology-driven models like Moveli’s broker network and established yet adaptable institutions like HTB. Borrowers and property developers may benefit from the wealth of experience these individuals bring to their new roles.

As the mortgage and property markets continue to evolve, such movements underscore the value of expertise and adaptability in meeting the needs of clients and customers alike.

item.title: Property buyers press ahead despite mortgage rate fears
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Prime London property markets have shown unexpected resilience in recent months, with transaction volumes holding steady despite mounting pressure on mortgage rates. According to Knight Frank's latest analysis, sales across prime central and outer London between June and August exceeded their five-year average by 2%, while year-on-year transactions rose by an impressive 18%.

Outer London leads market activity

Prime outer London (POL) has emerged as the standout performer, recording transactions 10% above the five-year average. This contrasts with prime central London (PCL), where sales remained 8% below average, though still showing a 6% improvement compared to the same period last year. Industry experts suggest this reflects shifting buyer priorities, with space and value becoming increasingly important considerations.

The figures are particularly noteworthy given the challenging financial backdrop. Government bond yields recently surpassed 5.2%, creating upward pressure on mortgage pricing. Tom Bill of Knight Frank notes: "Investor concerns about inflation risks and global debt burdens have driven borrowing costs higher across developed economies."

Budget stability supports market confidence

Market observers highlight the stabilising effect of reduced tax speculation ahead of this autumn's Budget. Unlike previous years filled with rumours of potential tax hikes, the current political climate has provided greater certainty for buyers. This relative calm has apparently encouraged both cash buyers and mortgage borrowers to proceed with property purchases.

Official figures paint a mixed picture of the wider market. While mortgage approvals dropped to their lowest level since January 2024 in July, residential transactions were only 1% below last year's figures and 4% higher than July 2024, according to HMRC data.

Looking ahead, potential challenges include the abolition of the non-dom tax regime and increased stamp duty surcharges on additional properties. However, current market behaviour suggests buyers are adapting to these uncertainties rather than retreating. Stuart Bailey of Knight Frank reports seeing more determined negotiation strategies rather than abandoned transactions.

As the market navigates these complex conditions, homeowners considering property moves might find it valuable to monitor both mortgage rate trends and potential tax changes. The coming months will reveal whether this current resilience can be maintained if financial pressures intensify further.

item.title: ‘Abolish landlords’ party deputy leader revealed as landlord
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The Green Party’s deputy leader has been revealed as a buy-to-let landlord, despite his party’s policies aiming to reduce private landlordism. Mothin Ali, co-deputy leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, owns two rental properties in Leeds through a private limited company, according to recent reports.

Property ownership details emerge

Ali, who serves as a Leeds city councillor, incorporated MA Holdings in December 2021 as the sole director. Property records show he purchased a three-bedroom former council house in Gipton for £165,000 in June 2022, followed by a second property in the same area for £157,000 in March 2023. Both homes reportedly have buy-to-let mortgages with tenants in residence.

The disclosure comes after Ali’s party adopted policies last year to discourage private landlordism through tax changes designed to make owning multiple rental properties less profitable. The Greens argue their approach would boost home ownership rates and reduce reliance on private rentals.

Party defends deputy leader's position

The Green Party has stated Ali’s property investments relate to caring responsibilities for vulnerable family members. A party spokesman commented: “Councillor Ali has acted solely in the interests of close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities.” The party declined to share further details, citing privacy concerns for Ali’s relatives.

This situation has drawn attention given the Green Party’s vocal criticism of the private rental sector. Party leader Zack Polanski previously described landlords as treating tenants like “cash cows” earlier this year. The Greens have advocated for significant reforms to rental market regulations and property taxation.

For homeowners considering buy-to-let investments, it may be worth reviewing how potential policy changes from different political parties could affect rental property finances. Those with existing portfolios might wish to stay informed about proposed tax adjustments that could impact profitability.

The revelation highlights the complex relationship between personal financial decisions and political ideologies, particularly in the housing sector. As parties develop policies affecting private landlords, both investors and tenants will be watching closely to understand how changes might influence the rental market.

item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH: Zoopla returns to profit as estate agent valuation leads jump
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Zoopla, one of the UK’s leading property portals, has announced a return to statutory profit alongside a significant rise in valuation leads for estate agents. According to its latest financial report, the platform generated 25% more valuation leads in 2025 compared to the previous year, with its best-performing product converting 43% of these leads into sales listings. These figures highlight Zoopla’s continued focus on helping estate agents connect with potential sellers.

Focus on Homeowner Engagement

Zoopla’s strategy increasingly centres on engaging homeowners long before they actively begin searching for their next property. In 2025, the number of homeowners tracking their property’s value through the portal rose by 39%, reaching 5.4 million by the end of the year. This figure has since grown to 6.4 million, demonstrating Zoopla’s ability to identify homeowners who may be preparing to sell. By monitoring property values and local market conditions, the platform uses this data to enhance its services and support its investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and conversational property search tools.

Financial Performance and Innovation

Despite a slight dip in revenue, from £84.2 million in 2024 to £83.2 million in 2025, Zoopla returned to statutory profitability, reporting a £20.7 million profit for the year. The company attributed the revenue decline to the completion of its product rationalisation process, which streamlined its offerings. Zoopla also achieved an operating margin of 16%, reflecting its efficient management and continued investment in its platform. Paul Whitehead, Zoopla’s chief executive, emphasised the company’s focus on delivering measurable returns for its partners through new multi-year partnerships with home builders, estate agents, and brand partners.

Whitehead commented, “Our strategy is working, which you can see in what we are delivering for our partners. Valuation leads to estate agents grew 25% year-on-year, and our best-performing product saw 43% of those leads convert into sales listings. Our approach is based on intent, not just volume.” He also highlighted the importance of Zoopla’s trusted relationship with homeowners, noting that many engage with the platform long before they enter the active search phase.

For homeowners considering selling their property, Zoopla’s tools and insights could prove invaluable in planning their next move. Meanwhile, estate agents may find the platform’s growing lead generation capabilities a useful resource in securing new listings.

item.title: House prices record first annual fall since 2023
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

House prices in the UK have experienced their first annual decline since November 2023, according to the latest Lloyds House Price Index. The average property price fell by 0.2% in August, following a similar 0.1% drop in July. This brings the average cost of a UK home to £298,468, down from £299,153 the previous month. On an annual basis, prices decreased by 0.4%, marking a notable shift in the housing market after nearly three years of steady growth.

Affordability Pressures Impact Buyer Activity

The housing market has faced increasing challenges in recent months, with affordability pressures and rising borrowing costs influencing buyer behaviour. Despite these obstacles, the overall decline in house prices remains modest, with values still 0.2% higher than at the start of the year. Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, noted that whilst the market has become more subdued, there has not been a widespread rush to reduce property prices. Instead, many sellers are choosing to hold firm, reluctant to accept offers they deem too low, whilst some buyers are adopting a wait-and-see approach as market conditions evolve.

Industry figures indicate that the number of homes changing hands has reached its lowest level since early 2024. However, it’s worth noting that average house prices remain approximately 25% higher than at the end of 2019, despite the significant rise in interest rates in recent years. Wage growth has helped to alleviate some affordability pressures, enabling the market to adjust gradually to higher borrowing costs.

Regional Variations Highlight North-South Divide

The performance of the housing market varies significantly across the UK, with northern regions continuing to outperform their southern counterparts. Northern Ireland, for example, recorded the strongest annual house price growth at 6.9%, reflecting a robust demand for property in the region. Conversely, more expensive southern markets have seen slower growth, with affordability constraints playing a key role in this divergence.

The regional disparity underscores the complexity of the UK housing market, where local economic conditions, employment rates, and buyer sentiment all contribute to varying levels of demand and price movement. Whilst some areas continue to see steady growth, others are experiencing a more pronounced slowdown as buyers and sellers navigate the challenges of higher interest rates and economic uncertainty.

Looking ahead, the market is expected to remain subdued in the coming months, with limited activity likely to keep house prices relatively stable. However, with employment holding up better than anticipated and wages continuing to grow, demand from those needing or wanting to move is expected to provide some support to the market. As always, prospective buyers and sellers may wish to carefully consider their options and seek professional advice to navigate the current landscape effectively.

item.title: Former Spicerhaart acquisitions director joins new M&A venture
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

A new mergers and acquisitions (M&A) venture targeting the UK property sector has been unveiled. Realise, launched by 2point0 Group, aims to provide tailored advice to estate and letting agency owners considering selling, merging, or acquiring businesses. The venture is spearheaded by Joel Osbourne, former national acquisitions director at Spicerhaart, who brings over 25 years of industry experience to the role.

Expertise at the Helm

Joel Osbourne joins Realise as a partner alongside co-founders Nicola and Paul Broomham. With a career spanning roles at LRG and Christie & Co, Osbourne has a proven track record in property acquisitions. During his tenure at Spicerhaart, he led national acquisition efforts, consolidating his reputation as a seasoned industry professional. Together, Osbourne and Paul Broomham have overseen more than 50 business sales, mergers, and acquisitions, ranging from small lettings firms to multi-million-pound corporate deals.

Realise is designed to support estate and letting agency owners looking to navigate the complexities of M&A. The venture will also assist firms seeking strategic growth through acquisitions or partnerships. This expansion complements 2point0 Group’s existing services, which include business consultancy and recruitment, further strengthening its offering to the property sector.

Industry Endorsements and Market Demand

The launch of Realise has garnered strong support from industry leaders. Michael Cook, CEO of LRG, praised Osbourne’s expertise, highlighting his ability to “create value” and deliver practical, experience-based advice. Similarly, Peter Fuller, a property industry veteran who has worked with both Osbourne and Broomham, commended their integrity and deep industry knowledge, describing them as “exceptionally well placed” for this new venture.

Nicola Broomham noted that the decision to expand into M&A was driven by significant demand from the sector. Since 2point0 Group’s inception earlier this year, the company has received numerous enquiries from estate and letting agency owners seeking specialist M&A guidance. Paul Broomham emphasised that Realise is focused on helping clients achieve their ambitions, stating, “It’s all about the outcome—the fulfilment of an ambition. Capitalising on the blood, sweat, tears, and investment that owners put into their businesses.”

With its blend of expertise, industry backing, and a clear focus on client outcomes, Realise is poised to become a key player in the UK property M&A landscape. For estate and letting agency owners considering their next steps, seeking specialist advice could be a strategic move to maximise value and achieve long-term success.

item.title: Government announces timetable for new property register
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The government has unveiled plans to introduce a national register for short-term and holiday lets in England, with the system expected to be fully operational by March 2027. Announced by Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy in Parliament, the register aims to provide councils with greater oversight of short-term accommodation in their areas. Whilst details remain under discussion, the register is likely to operate online and become mandatory for property owners and operators.

What Will the Register Involve?

The proposed register will require property owners to provide information about their short-term lets, including their number and location. This data will enable local authorities to better understand the impact of such properties on housing markets and enforce health and safety standards. However, key aspects of the scheme are still to be finalised, such as the frequency of registration and the body responsible for administering the system.

This initiative follows similar measures already in place in Scotland and Northern Ireland, while Wales is set to launch its visitor accommodation register in October 2026. The move comes amid growing concerns that the rise in short-term lets is reducing the availability of homes for long-term rent, particularly in tourist hotspots.

Industry Response and Local Flexibility

Industry body Propertymark has welcomed the register but emphasised the need for local councils to have flexibility in how the system operates. It argues that whilst short-term lets can boost tourism and offer property owners flexibility, councils require effective tools to address areas where high numbers of such lets are impacting housing availability for local residents.

Propertymark has previously called for greater parity between short-term lets and the private rented sector, advocating for proportionate regulation that reflects local housing market conditions. It also highlighted the importance of increasing the supply of private and social housing as a long-term solution to housing pressures. In its response to a government consultation in 2023, the organisation opposed additional measures in areas where short-term lets had no significant effect on private rental supply.

The body stressed the need for a balanced approach that supports both tourism and housing needs, with local councils best placed to determine whether such schemes are necessary in their areas. It also called for sufficient resources to ensure the register is implemented effectively, rather than being used to address historic funding gaps.

As the government works towards the 2027 deadline, homeowners operating short-term lets may wish to stay informed about the evolving requirements. With the register set to provide councils with valuable insights, it could play a key role in shaping the future of short-term accommodation in England.

item.title: Tributes paid to ‘titan of the property industry’
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property industry is mourning the loss of Mike Slade OBE, a towering figure whose career spanned decades and left an indelible mark on the sector. Slade, who passed away recently, was widely regarded as one of the most influential personalities in British property development. His leadership and entrepreneurial spirit transformed Helical, a company he was associated with for over three decades, into a major player in commercial, residential, and mixed-use projects.

A Legacy of Transformation

Mike Slade’s journey with Helical began in 1984 when he merged his private property business with Helical Bar, then a listed company primarily focused on manufacturing steel reinforcement. Under his stewardship, Helical evolved into a prominent property developer, a transformation that showcased Slade’s vision and determination. He served as chief executive for 35 years before taking on the role of chairman for a further three years, retiring in 2019 at the age of 72.

During his tenure, Slade’s innovative approach not only shaped Helical’s business strategy but also fostered a culture of entrepreneurship and collaboration. The company paid tribute to him, describing him as “one of the defining figures” in its history. His leadership style, characterised by energy and enthusiasm, inspired colleagues and peers alike, leaving a lasting legacy within the organisation.

Charitable Contributions and Industry Impact

Beyond his professional achievements, Mike Slade was deeply committed to charitable causes within the property industry. He played a pivotal role in LandAid, a charity dedicated to tackling homelessness, serving as president and helping to raise £20 million during his time with the organisation. Slade also chaired the fundraising appeal for the Oak Cancer Centre at The Royal Marsden in Sutton, which opened in 2023 following a £70 million campaign.

His dedication to philanthropy was matched by his generosity and passion for making a difference. Colleagues and industry leaders have highlighted his ability to inspire and bring people together, not just in business but also in support of meaningful causes.

Remembering a Titan

Tributes from across the property sector have poured in, celebrating Slade’s contributions and character. Robert Fowlds, chairman of Helical, described him as “a titan of the property industry,” praising his entrepreneurial spirit and the profound impact he had on both the business and the wider community. Matthew Bonning-Snook, Helical’s chief executive, recalled Slade’s infectious personality and boundless energy, which created a culture at Helical that many aspired to be part of.

Slade’s passing marks the end of an era for the property industry, but his legacy will continue to inspire future generations. His vision, leadership, and commitment to philanthropy have left an enduring imprint on the sector, and he will be greatly missed by all who had the privilege of knowing him.

As the property industry reflects on Mike Slade’s remarkable career, his contributions serve as a reminder of the profound impact one individual can have on both business and society. His legacy will undoubtedly endure, shaping the industry for years to come.

item.title: Rightmove launches new agent tool following Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Rightmove has introduced a streamlined rent review feature to its Tenancy Manager platform, helping letting agents adapt to regulatory changes under the Renters’ Reform Act. The new tool enables agents to generate and serve Section 13 rent increase notices directly within existing tenancy records, potentially reducing administrative burdens and improving compliance with rental legislation.

Simplifying rental administration

The update forms part of Rightmove's ongoing efforts to digitise and connect different stages of the lettings process. Agents can now manage rent reviews alongside other tenancy documentation within the same system, rather than maintaining separate processes. This integration could prove particularly valuable as the private rental sector navigates recent regulatory changes affecting tenancy agreements and rent adjustments.

Rightmove reports the rent review functionality was among the most requested improvements from letting professionals. By centralising these functions, the system aims to save time for agents while maintaining rigorous compliance standards.

  • Digital ID verification within Rightmove Referencing, allowing applicants to confirm their identity electronically
  • PEPs and sanctions screening for landlords, tenants and guarantors via Rightmove Plus
  • Further integration between different stages of the tenancy lifecycle

item.title: New approach could slash property transaction times
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New proposals could revolutionise the UK property market by dramatically speeding up transactions and reducing the number of collapsed sales. Recent analysis by LawtechUK, a Ministry of Justice-backed initiative, suggests that starting legal preparations earlier in the process may help achieve these long-sought improvements.

The case for early legal preparation

Traditionally, the conveyancing process only begins after a buyer is found, creating unnecessary delays. However, LawtechUK's research indicates that initiating legal work when a property is first listed could slash transaction times. Data from 500 test cases showed freehold properties reaching exchange in roughly 30 days, with leaseholds taking about 45 days - significantly quicker than current averages.

The early preparation model also appears to reduce fall-through rates to below 5%, compared to the national average of around 25-30%. This approach aligns with the government's Home Buying and Selling Reform Roadmap, which advocates for more upfront property information and greater use of digital technology throughout the transaction process.

How technology is transforming conveyancing

Several legal technology firms are already pioneering solutions that could make the home-moving process more efficient. These innovations include:

  • Automated due diligence checks
  • AI-assisted conveyancing tools
  • Real-time communication platforms
  • Shared transaction data systems

One such system, Conveyo, demonstrates how early legal instruction works in practice. When an estate agent lists a property, the seller immediately instructs a solicitor to gather all necessary legal documents. This preparation happens concurrently with the marketing period, rather than waiting for an offer to be accepted.

The potential benefits extend beyond speed. YouGov research commissioned by LawtechUK reveals that 27% of homebuyers find conveyancing causes prolonged stress, while 9% have considered abandoning purchases due to the anxiety involved. More efficient processes could help alleviate these pain points.

The road ahead for property reforms

While some changes will require legislation, many improvements can be implemented using existing technologies. The government's roadmap includes proposals for standardised sales packs prepared before marketing begins, along with standards for AI use in conveyancing.

For homeowners considering selling, these developments could mean less time between accepting an offer and completion. Estate agents may also benefit from reduced fall-through rates, allowing them to focus on progressing firm sales rather than rescuing collapsing chains.

As the property market continues to evolve, these technological and procedural advances could mark the beginning of a more efficient, less stressful home-moving experience for all parties involved.

item.title: Property TV presenter Kirstie Allsopp airlifted to hospital
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Property presenter Kirstie Allsopp has shared details of a serious accident that occurred during her recent birthday celebrations in Devon. The Channel 4 star, best known for co-presenting Location, Location, Location, was airlifted to hospital after slipping on a muddy path whilst walking back from a family picnic at Welcombe Mouth beach.

Emergency Response and Surgery

Following the fall, Kirstie’s 18-year-old son, Oscar, quickly sought help. Emergency services, including RNLI Bude Lifeboat paramedics and Cornwall Air Ambulance, were dispatched to assist. Kirstie was later transported to Barnstaple Hospital, where she underwent surgery for injuries sustained to her leg.

The presenter shared updates on social media, posting photographs of her bandaged leg and an X-ray taken after the operation. She also posted a picture from the ambulance, showing cuts to her face. Kirstie expressed her gratitude to the hospital staff, describing them as “amazing, kind and caring”. She added that she hoped to return home soon.

Reflection on the Incident

Kirstie described the accident as an unforgettable birthday experience, stating that it was “not a birthday I am going to forget”. The incident occurred during a family celebration, which included a picnic and swim at the picturesque Welcombe Mouth. Despite the ordeal, Kirstie remained positive, focusing on the swift response of the emergency teams and the support of her family.

As one of the UK’s most recognisable property experts, Kirstie’s accident has drawn attention from fans and well-wishers alike. Her openness about the incident has highlighted the importance of safety during outdoor activities, particularly in challenging terrain.

A Familiar Face in Property

Kirstie Allsopp has become a household name through her work on Channel 4’s Location, Location, Location, which she co-presents with Phil Spencer. The show, which has been on air for over two decades, has cemented her reputation as a trusted voice in the property market. Her recent accident serves as a reminder of the unexpected challenges life can bring, even during moments of celebration.

As Kirstie recovers from her injuries, fans will no doubt be eager to see her back on screen, continuing to guide viewers through the complexities of buying and selling homes. In the meantime, her positive outlook and gratitude for the support she received during the incident are a testament to her resilience.

item.title: New rental pricing tool targets costly mistakes under Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A new property technology tool aims to help letting agents and landlords set more accurate rental prices by analysing which homes prospective tenants reject during their property searches. Launched by proptech firm nHabit, the platform comes as agents adapt to stricter pricing rules under the Renters’ (Reform) Act.

How the rental pricing tool works

The innovative platform uses anonymised data from nHabit’s consumer property app, tracking not just properties renters show interest in, but also those they dismiss. By analysing rejection patterns across different postcodes and property types, the tool highlights where asking rents or property features may be deterring potential tenants.

Unlike traditional property portals that primarily track engagement, this system provides insights into rental demand sensitivity. Agents can access breakdowns showing whether rejections relate to price, location, property condition or other factors. The company suggests this could help landlords avoid overpricing properties before listing them on the market.

Changing landscape for rental pricing

The tool’s launch coincides with significant regulatory changes affecting the private rental sector. Since 1 May 2026, landlords and agents have been prohibited from accepting offers above the advertised rent under the Renters’ (Reform) Act. Combined with restrictions on rent increases and the abolition of Section 21 evictions, these changes make accurate initial pricing more crucial than ever.

Steven Charlton, founder of nHabit, commented: “We aim to understand renting like dating apps understand relationships. This level of insight comes from tracking both positive and negative responses to property listings.” The company reports its consumer app has been gaining 150-300 new London users daily since launching in February 2026.

What renters prioritise

Early data from the platform suggests renters consider multiple factors beyond headline rents when choosing properties. Location quality, transport links, property condition and long-term affordability all influence decision-making. The tool allows agents to see how these different elements affect tenant choices in specific areas.

For letting professionals, the potential benefit is clear – identifying unrealistic asking prices before properties struggle to attract interest in an increasingly regulated market. As the rental sector continues to evolve, such data-driven approaches may become more commonplace in helping landlords and agents navigate the changing landscape.

item.title: Property firms face £645m HMRC tax scrutiny
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) has significantly increased its scrutiny of major UK property firms, with potential additional tax liabilities under review reaching £645m for the 2025-26 financial year. This represents a 40% rise from £461m the previous year, according to data obtained by law firm Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner (BCLP). The figures highlight growing tax compliance efforts targeting Britain's largest property companies.

Increased HMRC focus on property sector taxation

The £645m figure relates to HMRC's "tax under consideration" metric - an estimate of maximum potential liabilities before full investigations conclude. These examinations fall under the Large Business Directorate, which oversees taxation for approximately 2,000 of the UK's biggest enterprises, including major listed property groups.

Industry analysts suggest this sharp increase reflects HMRC's broader compliance expansion. The tax authority recruited over 1,600 compliance officers during 2025-26, with plans to add 5,500 more by 2030. These staffing boosts contributed to HMRC exceeding £50bn in compliance yield for the first time last year.

Property companies might wish to review their tax positions carefully as this enhanced scrutiny continues. The sector's complex transactions and high-value assets often present multiple areas for potential tax disputes, particularly around corporate structures and cross-border arrangements.

Reduced clarity on tax treatment concerns businesses

Alongside increased investigations, BCLP's research reveals HMRC has become less willing to provide pre-transaction tax clarity. Freedom of Information data shows the tax authority rejected 41% of requests for tax treatment confirmation in 2025-26 - the highest refusal rate in five years.

The situation appears particularly challenging for corporation tax queries, where HMRC declined 63% of requests - more than double the previous 25-30% rejection rate. This shift could complicate business planning, as companies may face greater uncertainty when structuring major property transactions.

Tax specialists note that while HMRC's compliance drive aims to protect public finances, the reduced willingness to provide upfront guidance might lead to more disputes. Commercial property investors and developers may need to factor in potential delays when seeking tax certainty for complex deals.

As HMRC continues expanding its compliance operations, the property sector appears set for ongoing tax scrutiny. Businesses may wish to seek professional advice to ensure their tax affairs remain compliant whilst navigating this changing enforcement landscape.
